answer:
The name is a **genealogy chain**: each feature records which faces it derived from which previous faces, and the name reads as a path back to the originating sketch entity. Reading it inside-out ([inspect it](lab:face?name=shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]])):

1. **`base.outline.bottom`** — the sketch `base` has a rectangle `outline`; its `bottom` side line is the lowest edge of the sketch profile. The numbers (60 × 40 × 30) came from that line plus its siblings.
2. **`body/side[base.outline.bottom]`** — the `extrude` feature `body` swept that sketch profile; the lateral face generated from `outline.bottom` is named `body/side[…]`, with the source sketch entity in brackets. (`body/end` and `body/start` are the caps; side faces keep the sweep provenance.)
3. **`shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]`** — the `shell` feature hollows the box with the top (`body/end`) open. Each inner wall is the offset of one outer side face, so its name is `shell/inner[…]` with the outer face's whole name nested inside — you can see the whole history in one string.

You can confirm this yourself with `why()`: it reports exactly the two-step chain above (`shell: offset of body/side[…]` ← `body: swept from base.outline.bottom`).

Why it matters: these names are **persistent**, not positional. If you later fillet the corners or change `w` from 60 to 80, the face is still `shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]`, so a selector written against it — e.g. `j.feat('shell').faces()` filtered on that name, or an emboss/colour targeted at it — keeps resolving after edits. Contrast that with `.nth(i)`, which the compiler flags as `ref.fragile` precisely because an inserted feature can reshuffle the index.

No — it's **under by exactly 1 DOF**, and it's the hole the preset deliberately left free, `h2` (line 13 in [script.js](lab:open?file=script.js&line=13)).

Here's the solver arithmetic:

- The rectangle `l1–l4` is fully locked: `fix(l1.start)` anchors the chain, the four coincidences close the loop, horizontals/verticals kill the rotations, and `length(l1) = w`, `length(l2) = d` fix the sizes. Each of those lines reports `dof: 0`.
- Hole `h1` is fully constrained by its diameter plus distanceX/Y from the anchor corner ($2+1$ entity DOF $-$ rank 3 $= 0$).
- `h2` is a circle: 3 DOF (center.x, center.y, radius). It carries two constraints — `equal(h2, h1)` removes the radius DOF and `distanceY(h1.center, h2.center) = 0` removes center.y — so rank 2, leaving **1 DOF: `h2.center.x`**.

That's the intended design: the hole can slide left–right (within the plate) while staying at the same height and the same size as `h1`. If you wanted it fully constrained you'd add something like `j.c.distanceX('l1.start', 'h2.center')` (or `midpoint`/`symmetric`) in `.constrain(...)` — that would take the sketch from 1 DOF to 0. But since the brief calls for one hole left free to drag, I'd leave it as is.

It prints lying on its **back, on the −Y side** — the clip's side profile flat on the bed, with the 18 × 35 mm footprint down and the 12 mm height standing up. That's the auto orientation's choice:

**Why that way**

- **Zero supports.** Lying on −Y or +Y, the whole outline is the extrusion profile, so every wall is a vertical extrusion — no overhangs at all (0 mm³ of support). Turn it onto ±X and the jaw's lead-in overhangs by 134–134 mm³; onto ±Z and you'd need ~1.5 cm³ of support under the C-shaped jaw.
- **Solid bed contact.** 240 mm² of the flat side on the bed gives a stable, warp-resistant first layer — important for a clip that will see spring flexing in use.
- **Low height.** 12 mm tall, 60 layers, 12.1 min — quick to print and stiff in the layer direction where the grip matters... though note the flip side: layer lines run vertically through the jaw, so the flexing jaw faces inter-layer shear. For a first print of PETG that's acceptable; if you ever see cracking at the jaw root, printing on +X/−X (layers crossing the jaw) trades 134 mm³ of small supports for much stronger layers across the flex line.

The decision came from the print job's `'auto'` orientation, lexicographic on support → bed contact → height ([decision](lab:show?view=graph), [view](lab:view?name=side)).

The assembly's interference check reports it: look at the compile decisions (`program.decisions()`), which include one `gap` decision per pair of components, measured as the minimum distance between them:

- **pinion–wheel: ≈ 0.203 mm** ← the smallest gap, tooth flank to tooth flank
- base–pinion: ≈ 0.200 mm (the 0.6 mm spacer at $z = 4.0$ vs the axle port at $z = 4.8$)
- base–wheel: ≈ 0.200 mm

So the smallest clearance anywhere in the pair is the **~0.20 mm between the pinion's and the wheel's teeth**. That's not a coincidence: the mesh is assembled with the wheel jointed at 5° = $180°/36$, half a tooth, so a pinion tooth sits centred in a wheel gap, and the residual 0.203 mm is essentially the backlash that `j.lib.gear.spur` thins the teeth by under the default `backlash: 'fit'` class.

Two caveats on the number: it comes from the display meshes (the decision's reason says so; the exact B-rep distance is available with `{ exact: true }`, which I can't call from this eval scope — you'd see it in the compiler's own report), and it is the current-world minimum, i.e. at that 5° start pose. At other mesh phases the flank gap varies with the tooth profile, but the ~0.2 mm backlash class is what sets its scale. If you wanted more running clearance, `j.lib.gear.spur({ backlash: 'free' })` on both gears would widen it; the `j.inspect.gearMesh` contact ratio is the thing to re-check before committing.

One full turn of the 18-tooth pinion moves the rack by the pinion's **circumference at the pitch radius**:

$$\text{travel} = 2\pi r = \pi \cdot m \cdot z = \pi \cdot 2\ \text{mm} \cdot 18 = 36\pi \approx 113.10\ \text{mm}$$

The script's own numbers agree: `yc = mesh.pitchLineDistance = m·z/2 = 18 mm` ([script.js line 25](lab:open?file=script.js&line=25)), and the coupling rule in your notes — `travel = r × θ` in radians — gives $18 \times 2\pi = 113.10$ mm too. Equivalently, one tooth of pitch $p = \pi m = 6.283$ mm passes per $1/18$ turn, so per degree of crank it's $0.3142$ mm.

A practical side note: the rack is only 16 teeth long ($L = 16p \approx 100.5$ mm), so the rack runs out of teeth after about $100.5$ mm of travel — roughly 0.89 turns of the crank — before the pinion comes off the end. If you want the full-turn sweep usable, the rack needs at least 18–19 teeth.

1. **Print a coupon** — `j.fit.coupon({ kind: 'pin-hole', range: …, steps: 10 })` gives a graded hinge-style pin/hole part; print it, measure which gaps swing freely, and feed the rows to `j.fit.calibrate(rows)`. Note the model also adds the fit profile's hole compensation on top of the gap, so the modelled bore is Ø3 + 2·0.4 + hole comp; if you calibrate, that compensation gets measured too rather than the default 0.1 mm. Want me to add a fit coupon as a second print job in the script?

The side profile (the front view on the sheet — the sketch lives on XZ) is a **C-shape facing the desk**, drawn from the clip's working cross-section. Reading the outline [script.js](lab:open?file=script.js) from the top jaw down:

- **Top jaw** (`desk + t` at the top): a horizontal arm `jaw` (15 mm) long reaching *onto* the desk, with a **grip bump** at its tip — the outline steps in `jaw − 2 mm → grip → jaw − 4 mm`, so the last 2 mm pinches down 0.6 mm onto the desk's top face. The 1 mm ramp up to the tip (`jaw, desk + 1 mm`) is the **lead-in** the rule asks for: it guides the desk edge in when you push the clip on.
- **Spine** at `x = −t`: the vertical back, one wall thick (3 mm), the part you squeeze.
- **Bottom jaw**: a mirror arm under the desk, also ending in a `grip` bump with its own 1 mm lead-in (`jaw, −1 mm`).
- **Cable channel**: below the bottom jaw the outline folds under into a recessed lip — the under-hang between `cable + t` and `cable` forms an open channel `cable` (8 mm) tall that hangs beneath the desk edge and keeps cables from sliding off; the lip returns up via `−t − cable/2` so the wall never goes below 3 mm.

Everything is written as expressions of the five params (`desk`, `cable`, `w`, `t`, `jaw`, `grip`), so widening the desk or the cable channel moves the jaws and channel together — e.g. `desk + t` opens the top jaw and `−2*t − cable` keeps the back wall thickness invariant. The grip is 0.6 mm per side, inside your 0.4–0.8 mm fit band ([param desk](lab:param?name=desk)).

The extrusion is along the width `w` (12 mm), printed lying on its side — the side elevation is just the 12 × 35 rectangle, which is why the outline lies flat on the bed and the layers run along the spine, giving the clip its bending strength.

answer:
**The name is a genealogy, `<feature>/<role>[<source>]`, read from the outside in.** Nothing in it is a coordinate — it records which feature made the face and which face it came from, so it survives every edit that keeps that history.

```
shell / inner [ body / side [ base.outline.bottom ] ]
  │      │        │     │       │        │      └ sketch line 'outline.bottom'
  │      │        │     │       │        └ rect's side name (bottom/right/top/left)
  │      │        │     │       └ the rect entity id 'outline' (script.js:22)
  │      │        │     └ sketch id 'base' (script.js:21)
  │      │        └ extrude feature id 'body', role "side" (script.js:20–24)
  │      └ shell role "inner": the offset copy of that outer face
  └ shell feature id 'shell' (script.js:25)
```

Reading it backwards: the sketch `base` holds a rounded rect `outline`; `.rect()` labels its four straight sides `outline.bottom right top left` and its four corners `outline.br tr tl bl` (confirmed in the sketch record — the `bottom` line runs $(-27,-20)\to(27,-20)$, 54 mm long). The extrude `body` sweeps each of those profile edges into a side face, so the edge `outline.bottom` becomes `body/side[base.outline.bottom]` — the wall at $y=-20$, normal $-Y$, area $54\times30 = 1620\ \text{mm}^2$. The shell with open face `body/end` and `direction: 'in'` then offsets every *remaining* face inward by `wall`, and each new surface is named `shell/inner[<the face it was offset from>]`. Hence `shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]`: the inner wall opposite the bottom side wall.

`why()` shows the same chain the compiler used to resolve it: `shell/inner[…] ← shell: offset of body/side[…]` then `body/side[…] ← body: swept from sketch entity base.outline.bottom`.

Two details the numbers pin down: its normal is $+Y$, the reverse of its source's $-Y$, because an inner surface faces into the cavity; and its area is $54\times28 = 1512\ \text{mm}^2$ rather than 1620, the 2 mm `wall` shortening the cavity. Note the open face `body/end` is consumed by the shell, so its name no longer exists — the remaining originals are `shell/inner[body/start]` (the floor) and the four `shell/inner[body/side[…]]` walls.

Because the name is history and not geometry, changing `w`, `d` or `wall` at the sliders keeps it valid — [param](lab:param?name=w&value=80 mm) recompiles with the same faces. The one thing that breaks it is a change the offset can't do at all: `wall` 3 mm with the 3 mm corner radius `r` fails the shell outright (`feature.failed`, "reduce the thickness or remove small fillets first"), and then the name has no face to point at. See the feature at [shell](lab:node?id=shell) and the source line [script.js:25](lab:open?file=script.js&line=25); select it with [face](lab:face?name=shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]).

**It prints lying on its side — the side profile flat on the bed, layers stacking across the 12 mm width (build direction `-Y`).**

The compiler picked it by its orientation rule (`orient: 'auto'`, lexicographic: least support → most bed contact → least height). From the decision record:

| dir | support | bed contact | height |
|---|---|---|---|
| **−Y** | **0 mm³** | **240.4 mm²** | **12 mm** |
| +Y | 0 mm³ | 240.4 mm² | 12 mm |
| +X | 134.4 mm³ | 420 mm² | 18 mm |
| −Z | 1451.5 mm³ | 216 mm² | 35 mm |
| +Z | 1510.3 mm³ | 168 mm² | 35 mm |
| −X | 1638 mm³ | 48 mm² | 18 mm |

So: **no support anywhere** (overhang list empty, no `print.overhang` diagnostics at all), the whole side outline — $2884.8/12 = 240.4$ mm² — is the first layer, and the part is only 12 mm tall (60 layers at 0.2 mm, ≈12.1 min). Standing it "upright" (±Z, the desk edge vertical) would need 1.45–1.51 cm³ of support and 35 mm of height; turning it so the jaws point up (+X/−X) still needs 134–1638 mm³ because the jaw lead-ins and the channel hook then hang over air.

That is also the right print for the part, not just the cheapest: with the layers running parallel to the jaw length, the jaws' clamp flexure happens *in* the layer plane, so the pinch load never peels layers apart, and the spine's bend is likewise in-plane. The `+Y` row is numerically identical (it's the same body upside-down, since the outline is asymmetric only in the small grip bumps and lead-ins — both come out support-free); the tie was broken by the fixed order of candidate directions, so the mouth/lip side lands down.

The intent is written in the script too — see [script.js:80](lab:open?file=script.js&line=80): *"Printed on its side: the outline lies on the bed, so the layers run along the jaws and the spine bends with them."* Nothing in the current values (desk 18 mm, cable 8 mm, w 12 mm, t 3 mm, jaw 15 mm) or any slider range changes that — the clip stays support-free on its side as long as the outline is a single extruded profile, since every wall is then vertical with respect to `-Y`.

answer:
**One full turn of the pinion moves the rack $2\pi r = \pi m z = \pi \times 2 \times 18 = 113.10$ mm.**

That isn't my arithmetic alone — `j.inspect.gearMesh(pinion, rack)` in [script.js](lab:open?file=script.js&line=24) reports the mesh at module $m = 2$ mm, 18/16 teeth, pressure angle 20°, centre distance (pitch-line distance) **18 mm**, backlash 0.40 mm, and `travelPerTurn: 113.0973` (engine quantity, mm). The pinion's own bbox confirms the pitch radius: its body spans ±19.786 mm, i.e. $r + m = 18 + 2$ tip radius.

Two cautions, since the rule is travel = $r\theta$ with $\theta$ in radians:

- **The rack is shorter than one turn.** Its body is 100.53 mm long along X ($16 \times \pi \times 2$, the 16 theeth in the `rack` line) — so a full 360° turn overruns the toothed length by ~12.6 mm and the pinion would start climbing off the end. The usable stroke is ~100.5 mm, i.e. $100.53/113.10 = 0.889$ turn ≈ **320°**. Nothing in the script limits it: `.joint('travel', j.joint.slider(), …)` has no `limits`, so the coupling is yours to keep.
- **To pose it, use the coupling**, e.g. rack travel $d$ → `turn` $= d/18$ rad: 20 mm of travel is $20/18 = 1.111$ rad $= 63.66°$; 90° of crank is $18 \times \pi/2 = 28.27$ mm of rack. The assembly's `travel`/`turn` params ([script.js](lab:open?file=script.js&line=73)) both sit at 0, and since they aren't exposed in the Params view, a posed check goes through an override or a `check()` variant.

If you want, I can add `limits: [mm(-50), mm(50)]` to the slider and a `check()`-verified pose at `turn = 90°`/`travel = 28.27 mm` so the interference check runs at a meshed-offset pose rather than at zero.
